name: Karen and Coffee
description: To stay woke and attentive during classes, Karen needs some coffee! Karen, a coffee aficionado, wants to know the optimal temperature for brewing the perfect cup of coffee. Indeed, she has spent some time reading several recipe books, including the universally acclaimed "The Art of the Covfefe". She knows n coffee recipes. The i -th recipe suggests that coffee should be brewed between l i and r i degrees, inclusive, to achieve the optimal taste. Karen thinks that a temperature is admissible if at least k recipes recommend it. Karen has a rather fickle mind, and so she asks q questions. In each question, given that she only wants to prepare coffee with a temperature between a and b , inclusive, can you tell her how many admissible integer temperatures fall within the range?
input_specification: The first line of input contains three integers, n , k ( 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 200000 ), and q ( 1 ≤ q ≤ 200000 ), the number of recipes, the minimum number of recipes a certain temperature must be recommended by to be admissible, and the number of questions Karen has, respectively. The next n lines describe the recipes. Specifically, the i -th line among these contains two integers l i and r i ( 1 ≤ l i ≤ r i ≤ 200000 ), describing that the i -th recipe suggests that the coffee be brewed between l i and r i degrees, inclusive. The next q lines describe the questions. Each of these lines contains a and b , ( 1 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ 200000 ), describing that she wants to know the number of admissible integer temperatures between a and b degrees, inclusive.
output_specification: For each question, output a single integer on a line by itself, the number of admissible integer temperatures between a and b degrees, inclusive.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 816B — Karen and Coffee [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
